title: How to read Roman numerals
description: Learn the seven symbols, spot the subtraction pairs and turn a date such as MCMXLIV into a number you recognise.

sections.title: Get to know the seven symbols
sections.html:
Roman numerals turn up on clocks, buildings and film credits. A long string of letters can look intimidating, but the usual notation uses just seven symbols:

I = 1 · V = 5 · X = 10 · L = 50
C = 100 · D = 500 · M = 1,000

When the symbols run from larger to smaller values, add them. VI is 5 + 1, or 6. VIII is 5 + 1 + 1 + 1, or 8.

sections.title: When a smaller symbol comes first
sections.html:
Some pairs use subtraction. IV means 5 − 1, giving 4; IX means 10 − 1, giving 9. The standard pairs are IV, IX, XL, XC, CD and CM: 4, 9, 40, 90, 400 and 900.

You cannot use any pair you like. For example, 49 is written XLIX: forty plus nine. IL is not the standard form.

Historical inscriptions sometimes follow different conventions. Clock faces, for instance, often use IIII for four.

sections.title: Read a date one piece at a time
sections.html:
Take MCMXLIV. Split it into M | CM | XL | IV:

1,000 + 900 + 40 + 4 = 1944.

Breaking the date into thousands, hundreds, tens and units makes it easier to read and check.

What year is MMXXVI?

2026. MM is 2,000, XX is 20 and VI is 6.

sections.title: Three more to try
sections.html:
Work out XIV, XLII and XC. Look for subtraction pairs before adding the remaining values.

Show the answers
  • XIV = 10 + 4 = 14.
  • XLII = 40 + 2 = 42.
  • XC = 100 − 10 = 90.
